title: Finally ready for play testing!
author: Uncled1023
selftext:
Hi everyone!

Wanted to talk a bit about my new game, as well as the different processes I go through to get to this point.  And at the end, I have some questions I'd love your input on.

First off, I started with Codex, but then switched over to Claude once opus 5.5 was released, and haven't looked back.  I've found that it has been much better at actually listening to my thoughts on ui design, what to build, etc.  or at least, it listens better to how I talk and put forth ideas.  A couple things I found super helpful: 

- integration with blender.  Surprisingly I think I like making 3D games more than 2D currently with AI because it's much better at model making vs 2d sprite art.
- Suno's new MCP (it's amazing, especially for trailer design).  They just released a new version that includes 

A couple things that I've implemented that I think will help me, but I think can help you too.  I have a home server, so I added feedback functionality into the game that players can use, and it packages stats, logs, screenshots, etc and then sends it to my server.  Then the server connects to my discord to show me.  From there, it's super easy to have Claude then go through each issue or report and begin working on it.  I find it a really good async feedback and bug fixing system.  

If you'd like to take a look, feel free to try the play test here: https://store.steampowered.com/app/5455590/Heirs_to_the_Realm/


I would love your thoughts on a couple things:

- How do you handle performance testing on many devices?
- Anyone also dealing with pathing issues with large numbers of units on procedural terrain?  Any tips or articles you can show me?  I have it fairly good, but I feel like there is a more elegant solution out there.
- what kinds of pipelines do you all use for modeling?  Anything unique that might help model efficiency?

comments.author: ledniv
comments.body:
For the pathing, with large numbers of units I would try to make navigation a data problem rather than having every unit independently search the procedural terrain. Represent the traversable world as compact grid or region data, keep units referenced by indices, and only process the units that actually need a new path. If many units are moving toward the same destination, it can also be much cheaper to calculate shared navigation information once and let all of them use it rather than running a full search for every unit.

I actually made a free Data Oriented Design skill for coding agents that teaches a lot of these ideas around arrays, data locality, processing only relevant indices, and separating simulation from presentation:

[https://github.com/Data-Oriented-Design-for-Games/data-oriented-design](https://github.com/Data-Oriented-Design-for-Games/data-oriented-design)

Small plug: I cover the same ideas in much more depth in *High Performance Unity Game Development with Data Oriented Design*, including how data layout and architecture can make these kinds of large simulations much easier to optimize.

[https://www.manning.com/books/high-performance-unity-game-development](https://www.manning.com/books/high-performance-unity-game-development)

replies.author: Uncled1023
replies.body: Awesome, thank you for the reply!  I'll def take a look at those.  I'm kinda doing that kind of malling, with a few different pathing generators depending on the density/groupings.
